1:1.t: "Tent of meeting": the KJV's "tabernacle of the congregation", as in Exodus 27:21. The Hebrew ohel mo'ed means the tent where God meets with His people.

1:3.t: "So that it may be accepted": the KJV's "of his own voluntary will". The Hebrew can mean either; most modern Bibles read "that he may be accepted".

"Burnt offering" (Hebrew olah, "that which goes up"): the whole animal was burned and went up in smoke to God. It expressed complete dedication. The Greek translation, holokautoma, "wholly burned", gives the English word holocaust.

1:9.t: "Food offering": the KJV's "an offering made by fire". The Hebrew word (isheh) may be related to "fire" or to a word for "gift".

2:1.t: "Grain offering": the KJV's "meat offering", where "meat" meant food in general (see STYLE.md). No meat was in it.

3:4.t: "Lobe of the liver": the KJV's "caul above the liver", as in Exodus 29:13; the fatty lobe attached to the liver.

3:9.t: "Fat tail": the KJV's "rump", as in Exodus 29:22, from a breed of sheep with a broad fatty tail.

4:3.t: "Bringing guilt on the people": the KJV's "according to the sin of the people". The high priest's sin affected the whole nation he represented.
"The anointed priest" (Hebrew hakkohen hammashiach): mashiach, "anointed", is the word that gives us Messiah. Here it means the high priest, anointed with oil for his office (Exodus 29:7).

4:12.t: "Ceremonially clean": the KJV's "clean". Hebrews 13:11-12 sees in the burning outside the camp a picture of Jesus suffering outside the city gate.

5:1.t: "A public call to testify": the KJV's "hear the voice of swearing", a formal summons, under oath, for witnesses to come forward.

5:6.t: "Penalty": the KJV's "trespass offering". The Hebrew asham here means the penalty owed; from 5:15 on it names the guilt offering.

5:7.t: "Penalty": the KJV's "trespass offering". The Hebrew asham here means the penalty owed; from 5:15 on it names the guilt offering.

5:11.t: KJV: "the tenth part of an ephah".

5:15.t: "Of the proper value": the KJV's "with thy estimation by shekels of silver". The amount was set by valuation.

"Guilt offering" (Hebrew asham): the KJV's "trespass offering". It dealt with wrongs that could be counted and repaid, so it required restitution plus a fifth. Isaiah 53:10 says the Servant makes His life an asham.

"Acts unfaithfully" (Hebrew ma'al): the KJV's "commit a trespass". It means breaking faith, like a disloyal spouse or servant. Wronging a neighbor is also called unfaithfulness "against the LORD" (6:2).

6:1.t: In the Hebrew Bible these verses are 5:20-26, and 6:8-30 is 6:1-23.

6:9.t: "Hearth": the KJV's "the burning upon the altar".

6:20.t: KJV: "the tenth part of an ephah".

7:14.t: "Contribution", "presented": the KJV's "heave offering", as in Exodus 29:27-28, a portion lifted up and set apart for God and the priests.

7:32.t: "Contribution", "presented": the KJV's "heave offering", as in Exodus 29:27-28, a portion lifted up and set apart for God and the priests.
"Thigh": the KJV's "shoulder". The Hebrew shoq means the upper hind leg.

7:34.t: "Contribution", "presented": the KJV's "heave offering", as in Exodus 29:27-28, a portion lifted up and set apart for God and the priests.

7:18.t: "Credited": the KJV's "imputed". "Impure": the KJV's "an abomination"; the Hebrew piggul means spoiled or unfit meat.

7:37.t: "Ordination offering": the KJV's "consecrations", as in Exodus 29: the offering made when priests were installed in office (literally "filling the hand").

8:15.t: "Make atonement for it": the KJV's "to make reconciliation upon it".

9:24.t: "Shouted for joy": the KJV's "shouted". The Hebrew verb ranan means a ringing cry of joy.

10:6.t: "Do not let your hair hang loose": the KJV's "uncover not your heads", a sign of mourning.

11:5.t: "Rock badger": the KJV's "coney", the hyrax. The hyrax and hare do not chew cud as cattle do, but their chewing motion looks like it; the law describes animals as they appear.

11:13.t: Many of these birds cannot be identified with certainty, and modern Bibles differ. "Ostrich" (11:16) is the KJV's "owl"; "hoopoe" (11:19) is the KJV's "lapwing".

11:20.t: "Flying insects": the KJV's "fowls that creep". The Hebrew means winged swarming things.

11:29.t: The KJV's "tortoise", "ferret", "snail" and "mole" are probably kinds of lizards; the identifications are uncertain.

12:2.t: "Monthly period": the KJV's "the days of the separation for her infirmity".

12:5.t: "Monthly period": the KJV's "the days of the separation for her infirmity".

12:8.t: Mary offered the poor family's offering of two birds after Jesus' birth (Luke 2:22-24).

13:2.t: "Rash": the KJV's "scab". 13:30 "Scaly itch": the KJV's "dry scall".

"Serious skin disease" (Hebrew tsara'at): the KJV's "leprosy". The word covers a range of skin conditions, and also mold in cloth (13:47) and in houses (14:34). It is not the same as modern leprosy (Hansen's disease), whose symptoms do not match these descriptions. The priest acted as an inspector of ritual cleanness, not as a physician. In the Gospels Jesus touches and heals people with this disease (Mark 1:40-42), and the Greek lepra carries the same broad meaning.

13:45.t: "Cover the lower part of his face": the KJV's "put a covering upon his upper lip".

13:47.t: "Spreading mold": the KJV's "plague of leprosy" in a garment. "Destructive": the KJV's "fretting". "Woven or knitted": the KJV's "warp, or woof"; the exact meaning is uncertain.

14:5.t: "Fresh water": the KJV's "running water", literally "living water", water from a spring or stream.

14:50.t: "Fresh water": the KJV's "running water", literally "living water", water from a spring or stream.

14:10.t: KJV: "three tenth deals of fine flour" and "one log of oil". 14:21 KJV: "one tenth deal".

14:34.t: "Spreading mold" in a house: the KJV's "plague of leprosy in a house". The Hebrew tsara'at, the KJV's "leprosy", covers a range of skin conditions and also mold in cloth and in houses; it is not the same as modern leprosy (Hansen's disease). See 13:2.

15:2.t: "Discharge": the KJV's "running issue", an abnormal discharge from the genitals.

15:25.t: The woman Jesus healed in Mark 5:25-34, who had bled for twelve years, lived under this law.

16:2.t: "Most Holy Place": the KJV's "holy place within the vail". In this chapter "the holy place" usually means the inner room.

16:21.t: "A man appointed for the task": the KJV's "a fit man".

16:29.t: The seventh month is September to October. This is Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.
"Humble yourselves" (Hebrew innitem et-naphshotekhem): the KJV's "afflict your souls". It came to mean fasting (Psalm 35:13, Isaiah 58:3), and Acts 27:9 calls this day "the Fast".

17:7.t: "Goat idols": the KJV's "devils". The Hebrew se'irim means "goats" or "hairy ones", goat-demons thought to live in the wilderness.

18:6.t: "Have sexual relations with": the KJV's "uncover the nakedness of", a Hebrew idiom for sexual intercourse.

18:21.t: "Give any of your children to be offered as a sacrifice to Molech": the KJV's "let any of thy seed pass through the fire to Molech". Molech was a god worshiped with child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10, Jeremiah 32:35).

18:23.t: "Perversion": the KJV's "confusion"; the Hebrew tevel means a mixing of what should be kept apart.

19:16.t: "Endanger your neighbor's life": the KJV's "stand against the blood of thy neighbour". It may also mean "do not stand idly by when your neighbor's life is in danger".

19:20.t: "There must be an inquiry": the KJV's "she shall be scourged". The Hebrew word is rare and may mean an inquiry, compensation, or punishment.

19:26.t: "Divination ... omens": the KJV's "enchantment ... observe times", seeking hidden knowledge or lucky days.

19:31.t: "Mediums ... spiritists": the KJV's "them that have familiar spirits ... wizards", people who claimed to consult the dead.

19:35.t: "Length": the KJV's "meteyard", a measuring rod. "Dry measure ... liquid measure": the KJV's "a just ephah, and a just hin".

20:9.t: "His blood will be on his own head": the KJV's "his blood shall be upon him", meaning he is responsible for his own death.

20:12.t: "Perversion": the KJV's "confusion", as at 18:23; the Hebrew tevel means a mixing of what should be kept apart.

20:18.t: "During her monthly period": the KJV's "having her sickness".

21:6.t: "Food of their God": the KJV's "bread of their God". It means the offerings, not that God eats.

21:8.t: "Food of their God": the KJV's "bread of their God". It means the offerings, not that God eats.

21:17.t: "Food of their God": the KJV's "bread of their God". It means the offerings, not that God eats.

"Defect" (Hebrew mum): the same word is used for animals that cannot be offered (22:20). The priest, like the sacrifice, was to picture wholeness before God. A priest with a defect was not unclean and still ate the holy food (21:22). Hebrews 7:26 describes Christ as the priest who is "holy, blameless, unstained".

21:7.t: "A woman defiled by prostitution": the KJV's "a whore, or profane"; the Hebrew may mean two kinds of women.

21:14.t: "A woman defiled by prostitution": the KJV's "a whore, or profane"; the Hebrew may mean two kinds of women.

21:18.t: Several of these Hebrew terms are rare, and the conditions cannot be identified precisely.

22:10.t: "Guest": the KJV's "a sojourner of the priest".

23:7.t: "Regular work": the KJV's "servile work", the ordinary work of one's trade.

23:13.t: KJV: "two tenth deals" (two tenths of an ephah) of flour; "the fourth part of an hin" of wine.

23:17.t: KJV: "two tenth deals" (two tenths of an ephah) of flour; "the fourth part of an hin" of wine.

24:5.t: KJV: "two tenth deals" (two tenths of an ephah) of flour; "the fourth part of an hin" of wine.

23:16.t: The Festival of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, is called Pentecost in Greek (Acts 2:1), from the word for "fiftieth".

23:24.t: The first day of the seventh month later became Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year.

23:34.t: "Booths": the KJV's "tabernacles", temporary shelters of branches (Sukkot).

23:40.t: "Fruit of beautiful trees": the KJV's "boughs of goodly trees". The Hebrew peri means fruit.

24:11.t: "The Name": the Hebrew says only "the Name", meaning the LORD's name (24:16).

"Blasphemed" (Hebrew naqav): to pierce, and so to pronounce or to curse. Later Jewish tradition read this verse as forbidding the pronunciation of the divine name at all. That is why readers said Adonai, "Lord", instead of God's personal name YHWH (probably pronounced Yahweh), and why the KJV prints it LORD in capitals (see Genesis 2:4).

24:12.t: "The will of the LORD should be made clear": the KJV's "the mind of the LORD might be shewed them".

25:5.t: "Untended vines": the KJV's "thy vine undressed". The Hebrew nazir, "consecrated" or "unpruned", is the same word as Nazirite (Numbers 6), whose hair was also left uncut.

25:9.t: "Ram's horn": the KJV's "trumpet of the jubile"; the Hebrew is shofar.

25:34.t: "Pastureland": the KJV's "the field of the suburbs".

25:36.t: "Interest ... profit": the KJV's "usury, or increase". "Usury" once meant any interest at all, not only excessive interest. See Exodus 22:25.

25:44.t: These verses allowed Israelites to own foreign slaves, while forbidding the permanent enslavement of fellow Israelites. The Law also limited how slaves could be treated (Exodus 21:20-27, Deuteronomy 23:15-16).

26:1.t: "Sacred pillar": the KJV's "standing image". "Carved stone": the KJV's "image of stone".

26:16.t: "Wasting disease, and fever": the KJV's "consumption, and the burning ague".

26:30.t: "Incense altars": the KJV's "images". The Hebrew chammanim may be incense altars or sun pillars.

26:34.t: 2 Chronicles 36:21 says the exile fulfilled this, giving the land its missed Sabbaths for seventy years.

27:3.t: KJV: fifty, thirty, twenty, ten, five, three and fifteen shekels.

27:16.t: KJV: "an homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver".

27:25.t: A gerah is about 0.6 grams; see Exodus 30:13.

1:2.t: "Offering" (Hebrew qorban): from qarab, "to come near". An offering is literally "something brought near" to God, and the worshiper comes near with it. Jesus uses the word in Mark 7:11.

1:4.t: "Lay his hand" (Hebrew samakh, "lean on"): the worshiper pressed his hand on the animal's head, identifying himself with it as his substitute. The same act appears on the Day of Atonement (16:21).

"Make atonement" (Hebrew kipper): to make atonement means to remove guilt and defilement so that the relationship with God is restored. The root may mean "to cover" or "to wipe clean", and it is related to "ransom" (kopher); the English word was coined from "at one-ment", being made one with God. See Exodus 29:33. This is the first use of the word in Leviticus, which uses it about fifty times.

2:2.t: "Memorial portion" (Hebrew azkarah): the part of the grain offering burned on the altar, from zakhar, "remember". It may mean the portion that calls the worshiper to God's remembrance. Acts 10:4 echoes the idea: "your prayers and gifts have gone up as a memorial before God."

2:13.t: "Salt of the covenant": salt preserves and was used at covenant meals. A "covenant of salt" means a lasting, unbreakable covenant (Numbers 18:19, 2 Chronicles 13:5).

3:1.t: "Peace offering" (Hebrew shelamim, from shalom): shalom means peace, wholeness, and well-being with God and others. This was the one sacrifice the worshiper ate, sharing a meal in God's presence. Some modern Bibles call it the "fellowship offering".

3:17.t: "Blood": the reason is given at 17:11: the life of a creature is in its blood, and God gave it for atonement. See also Genesis 9:4.

4:2.t: "Unintentionally" (Hebrew bishgagah, "by straying"): the KJV's "through ignorance". It covers sins committed by mistake or without realizing it was a sin. Deliberate, defiant sin ("with a high hand") is treated differently (Numbers 15:27-31).

"Sins" (Hebrew chata): the most common word for sin, meaning to miss the mark, as a slinger misses a target (Judges 20:16). The other two main words for sin are avon, twisting or wrongdoing, and pesha, revolt or rebellion (see Exodus 34:7).

4:20.t: "They will be forgiven" (Hebrew nislach): the verb salach is used only of God forgiving, never of people forgiving one another. The sacrifices are the means; God is the one who forgives.

5:5.t: "Confess" (Hebrew hitvaddah): to acknowledge openly. Confession had to come with the offering; the ritual was not a substitute for repentance.

6:2.t: "Acts unfaithfully" (Hebrew ma'al): the KJV's "commit a trespass". It means breaking faith, like a disloyal spouse or servant. Wronging a neighbor is also called unfaithfulness "against the LORD" (6:2).

7:12.t: "Thanks" (Hebrew todah): the word means both thanks and confession, acknowledging what God has done. The thank offering was given after God answered prayer or rescued someone (Psalm 107:22, 116:17). Hebrews 13:15 calls praise "the sacrifice of praise".

7:16.t: "Freewill offering" (Hebrew nedavah): an offering given voluntarily, not because of a vow or a duty. The same root describes the willing gifts for the tabernacle (Exodus 35:29).

7:20.t: "Belonging to the LORD": the peace offering was a meal shared in God's presence, so eating it while unclean treated holy things as common. Paul draws on this in 1 Corinthians 11:27-29.

8:12.t: "Anointed" (Hebrew mashach): to pour or smear with oil to set someone apart for an office. The related word mashiach, "anointed", gives us Messiah; 4:3 uses it of the high priest. Oil was poured on Aaron's head, the first anointing of a person in the Bible. Psalm 133:2 recalls it.

8:23.t: Ear, thumb and toe: the blood marked the whole person for God's service, hearing, doing and walking.

10:1.t: "Unauthorized fire" (Hebrew esh zarah, "strange fire"): fire not taken from the altar, or offered in a way God had not commanded. The text does not say exactly what was wrong; the warning against drinking in 10:9 may hint that drunkenness was involved.

10:3.t: "I will show Myself holy ... I will be honored" (Hebrew eqqadesh ... ekkaved): God reveals His holiness and glory either by blessing those who approach Him rightly or by judging those who treat Him carelessly.

10:10.t: "Holy and common, unclean and clean": the four key categories of Leviticus. "Holy" (qodesh) is what belongs to God; "common" (chol) is ordinary. "Clean" (tahor) is fit to approach God; "unclean" (tame) is not. Unclean does not mean sinful: touching a dead body or giving birth made a person unclean without any sin.

11:10.t: "Detestable" (Hebrew sheqets): the KJV's "abomination". This word is used for unclean food and differs from to'evah, the stronger word for moral abominations (18:22).

11:44.t: "Be holy, because I am holy" (Hebrew qedoshim tihyu ki qadosh ani): the central theme of Leviticus, repeated at 19:2, 20:26. Holiness means being set apart for God and sharing His character. Peter quotes it in 1 Peter 1:16. Jesus later declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Acts 10 shows the food laws no longer separate Jew from Gentile; the call to holiness remains.

13:3.t: "Pronounce him unclean" (Hebrew time'o): literally "declare him unclean". The priest did not cause the condition; he gave a ruling about it, which decided whether the person could join in worship and community life.

13:46.t: "Outside the camp": the place of uncleanness and separation from God's dwelling. Hebrews 13:12-13 applies the phrase to Jesus, who "suffered outside the gate", and calls His followers to go to Him there.

14:4.t: "Hyssop" (Hebrew ezov): a small aromatic plant, probably a kind of marjoram, used as a brush for sprinkling. It was used at the first Passover (Exodus 12:22), and David prays, "Purge me with hyssop" (Psalm 51:7).

14:7.t: The released bird: one bird died and the other went free, carrying away the uncleanness, much like the goat on the Day of Atonement (16:21-22).

15:31.t: "Uncleanness": these laws treat bodily discharges, especially those connected with life and death, as making a person unfit to approach God's dwelling, not as sinful. They taught that God's presence demanded wholeness and life. The sin offering here (15:15, 15:30) is a purification offering, not a penalty for wrongdoing: the Hebrew chatta't means both "sin" and the offering that deals with sin, and its main purpose was to purify the sanctuary and the worshiper from defilement (see Exodus 29:14).

16:8.t: "Scapegoat" (Hebrew la'aza'zel, "for Azazel"): the meaning is debated. It may be (1) a name for a wilderness demon, opposite "for the LORD"; (2) "the goat that goes away"; or (3) "for complete removal". The KJV, following Tyndale, who coined the English word "scapegoat", took the second view. Whatever the word means, the point is clear in verses 21-22: Israel's sins were carried away, never to return.

16:16.t: "Rebellious acts" (Hebrew pesha'im): the KJV's "transgressions", meaning revolt against God. Unlike the sin offerings of chapter 4, which dealt with unintentional sins, the Day of Atonement cleansed even deliberate rebellion. The three main Hebrew words for sin are avon (twisting, wrongdoing), pesha (revolt) and chatta'ah (missing the mark); see Exodus 34:7.

16:30.t: "Cleanse you" (Hebrew letaher): atonement here removes not only guilt but the defilement sin leaves behind. Hebrews 9-10 reads this chapter as a picture of Christ, the high priest who entered the true Most Holy Place "once for all" with His own blood.

17:11.t: "The life of a creature is in the blood" (Hebrew nephesh habbasar baddam hi): nephesh here means life. The word means a living, breathing creature, a whole person, not a soul separate from the body, and is translated soul, life, person or self depending on the setting (see Genesis 2:7). The verse explains why blood was not to be eaten and why it atoned: a life was given in place of a life. "Because of the life in it" can also be read "by means of the life" or "in exchange for the life". Hebrews 9:22 summarizes: "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness."

18:5.t: "Will live by them" (Hebrew vachai bahem): obeying God's laws leads to a full life under His blessing. Paul quotes this verse twice (Romans 10:5, Galatians 3:12) to contrast righteousness by keeping the law with righteousness by faith.

18:22.t: "Detestable" (Hebrew to'evah): the KJV's "abomination", the strongest Hebrew word for what God finds repugnant. It is used of idolatry (Deuteronomy 7:25), child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31), dishonest weights (Deuteronomy 25:16), and pride and lying (Proverbs 6:16-19), as well as of the sexual practices in this chapter. It differs from sheqets, a weaker word used for unclean foods (see 11:10).

19:2.t: "Be holy, because I am holy": the central theme of Leviticus (see 11:44-45). Holiness means being set apart for God and sharing His character. This chapter shows what holiness looks like in everyday life: honoring parents, caring for the poor, honest business, fair courts, and love of neighbor stand next to ritual laws.

19:9.t: "Gleanings" (Hebrew leqet): what was dropped or left behind by the harvesters. The poor had a right to it. Ruth gleans in Boaz's field under this law (Ruth 2).

19:18.t: "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Hebrew ve'ahavta lere'akha kamokha): ahav covers love of every kind, between family members, friends, spouses, and between God and His people (see Genesis 22:2). Here it means acting for another's good, shown in the commands around it: no revenge, no grudges, no hatred in the heart. Jesus calls this the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39), and in the parable of the Good Samaritan answers "Who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29-37). Verse 34 extends the same love to the foreigner.

19:28.t: "Tattoo marks" (Hebrew ketovet qa'aqa): the KJV's "print any marks upon you". The phrase appears only here, beside cutting for the dead, so it likely refers to mourning or pagan religious marks.

20:2.t: "Stone him": stoning was carried out by the community together, so that the whole people took responsibility for removing evil from among them (Deuteronomy 17:7). Jesus refused to condemn the woman caught in adultery under 20:10 (John 8:3-11).

20:27.t: "Stone him": stoning was carried out by the community together, so that the whole people took responsibility for removing evil from among them (Deuteronomy 17:7). Jesus refused to condemn the woman caught in adultery under 20:10 (John 8:3-11).

22:32.t: "I must be acknowledged as holy" (Hebrew niqdashti): the same verb as 10:3. Israel was to show the world what God is like; profaning His name means bringing dishonor on Him. Compare "Hallowed be Your name" (Matthew 6:9).

23:2.t: "Appointed festivals" (Hebrew mo'adim): times set by God for meeting with His people, from the same root as ohel mo'ed, "tent of meeting". "Sacred assembly" (miqra qodesh): a holy gathering called by proclamation; the KJV's "holy convocation".

23:10.t: "Firstfruits" (Hebrew reshit): the first and best of the harvest, given to God as a pledge that the whole harvest is His. Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20), since He rose on the day after the Sabbath of Passover week, the day this sheaf was waved.

23:36.t: "Closing assembly" (Hebrew atseret): the KJV's "solemn assembly". It comes from a verb meaning to hold back or close. On "the last day, the great day of the feast" Jesus cried out, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink" (John 7:37).

24:20.t: "Eye for eye": this law set a limit on punishment in the courts, so that it would match the injury and not exceed it. It was not permission for personal revenge, and payment could often take the place of injury. See Exodus 21:23-25. Verse 22 stresses equal justice for foreigner and native alike.

25:10.t: "Jubilee" (Hebrew yovel): the word means a ram or ram's horn, the horn blown to announce the year. "Liberty" (deror) means release, the freeing of slaves and the return of land. Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1-2, which draws on this chapter, in the synagogue at Nazareth: "to proclaim liberty to the captives ... to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor" (Luke 4:18-19). The words "Proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof" are cast on the American Liberty Bell.

25:23.t: "The land is Mine": the land belonged to God, and Israel held it as tenants. This is why land could only be leased until the Jubilee, never sold forever. "Foreigners and residents" (gerim vetoshavim) describes Israel's standing before God; 1 Peter 2:11 applies the same words to believers.

25:25.t: "Nearest relative ... redeem" (Hebrew go'el, ga'al): ga'al means to buy back or rescue as a family member. The go'el, the kinsman-redeemer, was the relative who bought back land or a relative sold into debt, or avenged a kinsman's blood (see Exodus 6:6). Boaz acts as go'el for Ruth and Naomi (Ruth 4), and Job declares, "I know that my Redeemer lives" (Job 19:25).

25:39.t: "Slave" (Hebrew eved): the same word means servant or slave. The Law distinguishes a poor Israelite working off a debt, to be treated as a hired worker and freed at the Jubilee, from a permanent slave. Verses 42 and 55 give the reason: Israel already belongs to God as His servants.

26:11.t: "I will put My dwelling place among you ... I will walk among you" (Hebrew mishkani; hithallakhti): the language recalls God walking in the garden (Genesis 3:8) and the tabernacle (Exodus 25:8). Paul quotes verse 12 in 2 Corinthians 6:16, and Revelation 21:3 uses it of the new creation.

26:41.t: "Uncircumcised hearts" (Hebrew levavam he'arel): hearts closed to God, like a foreskin that has not been removed. The remedy is a circumcised heart (Deuteronomy 10:16, 30:6, Jeremiah 4:4, Romans 2:29).

26:44.t: Even after judgment, God will not break His covenant. The chapter ends not in destruction but in a promise to remember.

27:2.t: "Special vow" (Hebrew yaphli neder): a vow made to God. Persons were dedicated to God's service by paying their value, as Hannah later gave Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11).

27:28.t: "Devoted" (Hebrew cherem): something devoted was handed over entirely to God, either for the sanctuary or for destruction, and could not be kept for personal use or bought back (see Exodus 22:20). Verse 29 refers to people placed under God's judgment, as in the conquest of Canaan; it did not allow anyone to devote another person to death by his own vow.

27:30.t: "A tenth" (Hebrew ma'aser): the KJV's "tithe". Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek (Genesis 14:20), and Jacob promised one (Genesis 28:22). Malachi 3:8-10 rebukes Israel for withholding it.
